docs/getting-started.html.summary: Getting started This guide shows the quickest way to start using UtilityKit in a .NET project, plus instructions for building the library locally and running tests. Prerequisites .NET SDK (recommended: .NET 6, .NET 7, or later) A code editor (Visual Studio / VS Code / Rider) Optional: docfx to build documentation locally Install via NuGet The package on NuGet is published as UtilityKit. Replace x.y.z with the version you want to use. dotnet CLI dotnet add package UtilityKit --version x.y.z PackageReference <PackageReference Include="UtilityKit" Version="x.y.z" /> If you want to depend on the local project during development, add a project reference instead of the package. Quick usage examples Add the namespace (actual types may vary — check the API reference produced by DocFX): using UtilityKit; public class QuickExamples { public void Run() { // 1. Safe string helpers string input = " hello "; var trimmed = StringHelpers.TrimOrNull(input); // "hello" // 2. Guard helpers: argument validation Guard.NotNull(input, nameof(input)); // 3. DistinctBy: collection helper (LINQ-style) var users = new List<User> { /* ... */ }; var uniqueByEmail = users.DistinctBy(u => u.Email).ToList(); // 4. Date/time helper: get UTC ISO string var nowUtcIso = DateTime.Now.ToUtcIsoString(); // e.g. "2026-01-09T12:34:56Z" // 5. JSON helpers var json = JsonHelpers.Serialize(users); var deserialized = JsonHelpers.Deserialize<List<User>>(json); } } Note: The examples above demonstrate typical usage patterns. Consult the API reference for exact type and method names available in the version you install. Add to a project (example) Create a new console app and add UtilityKit: dotnet new console -n MyApp cd MyApp dotnet add package UtilityKit --version x.y.z Use helpers: using UtilityKit; Console.WriteLine(StringHelpers.TrimOrNull(" sample ")); Build from source If you want to build UtilityKit locally or contribute, follow these steps: Clone the repository: git clone https://github.com/siddiquiaslam/UtilityKit.git cd UtilityKit Restore dependencies and build: dotnet restore dotnet build -c Release (Optional) Create a local NuGet package: dotnet pack -c Release -o nupkg You can then install the generated .nupkg into your projects or publish to a local feed. Run tests Unit tests are included in the repository (if present). Run them with: dotnet test If tests require specific runtimes or environment variables, check the test project's README or the repository's CI configuration. Working with specific frameworks UtilityKit aims to target commonly used .NET frameworks (for example, net6.0, net7.0, or netstandard2.0) so it can be reused in libraries and apps. If you encounter compatibility issues: Ensure your app's target framework is compatible with the UtilityKit package version you're using. If building from source, inspect project files (.csproj) for target frameworks and adjust as needed. Troubleshooting "NU1101: Package not found" — verify the package id and version, or use a local .nupkg produced via dotnet pack. "Type or namespace name 'UtilityKit' does not exist" — confirm using statement and that the package/reference is added to the correct project. Platform-specific APIs — some helpers may target modern .NET runtimes. If you need legacy framework support, check the project's supported TFMs or open an issue. docs/introduction.html.title: Introduction | UtilityKit
docs/introduction.html.summary: Introduction UtilityKit is a lightweight, extensible collection of helper classes and extension methods created to simplify common development tasks in .NET applications. It provides small, focused utilities for date/time handling, string manipulation, collections, I/O, serialization, validation, and other recurring patterns so you don't have to rewrite boilerplate logic. This documentation site contains conceptual articles and full reference API documentation generated with DocFX. Use the navigation at the left (or the table of contents) to explore conceptual guides, examples, and detailed type/method reference pages. Goals Reduce boilerplate for common tasks (formatting, parsing, validation, etc.) Provide clear, well-tested utility APIs that are easy to discover and use Be small and composable so you can take only what you need Follow .NET conventions (extension methods, clear naming, immutable-friendly where appropriate) Who should use UtilityKit Application developers who want small, reliable helpers instead of writing small utilities repeatedly Library authors who prefer composable, well-named helper APIs Teams looking to centralize common helpers into a shared dependency What's included (high level) Date/time helpers and extension methods (parsing, formatting, time zone helpers) String utilities (safe trimming, null/empty handling, formatting helpers) Collection extensions (safe enumerations, paging helpers, deduplication) Guard and validation helpers (argument validation helpers to reduce guard clauses) I/O and file helpers (path helpers, temp file helpers) JSON and serialization helpers (convenience wrappers around System.Text.Json or Newtonsoft.Json) Convenience wrappers and extension methods to make common code more readable See the API reference for a complete, up-to-date list of types, methods, and samples. Quickstart Install the package from NuGet (replace with the exact package id if necessary): dotnet CLI dotnet add package UtilityKit PackageReference <PackageReference Include="UtilityKit" Version="x.y.z" /> Then reference it in your code: using UtilityKit; // Example: safe string trimming var name = StringHelpers.TrimOrNull(someInput); // Example: collection helper var distinct = items.DistinctBy(x => x.Id); // Example: guard Guard.NotNull(user, nameof(user)); Note: The examples above show typical patterns. Refer to the API reference for exact type and method names. Examples A simple example that demonstrates a couple of common patterns: using UtilityKit; public class Example { public void Run() { // Safe parsing / formatting var ts = DateTime.Now.ToUtcIsoString(); // -> "2026-01-09T12:34:56Z" // Guard helpers reduce boilerplate checks Guard.NotNull(input, nameof(input)); // Collection extensions var unique = users.DistinctBy(u => u.Email).ToList(); // Serialization convenience var json = JsonHelpers.Serialize(user); var deserialized = JsonHelpers.Deserialize<User>(json); } } Again, see the reference for exact member names and overloads. It provides focused utilities for common tasks such as date/time handling, string and collection helpers, argument guards, serialization helpers, and other repeatable patterns so you can write clearer, smaller code without reimplementing the same small utilities. Use this documentation site to learn how to install and use UtilityKit, read conceptual guides and recipes, and browse the generated API reference. Quick install Install the latest stable package from NuGet: dotnet add package UtilityKit Or add a PackageReference: <PackageReference Include="UtilityKit" Version="x.y.z" /> Replace x.y.z with the specific version you want to use. Highlights Small, composable helpers that follow .NET conventions Extension methods for common types to keep call sites expressive Guard and validation helpers to reduce repetitive argument checks Serialization and JSON convenience wrappers Collection and LINQ-style helpers like DistinctBy, paging helpers, etc. Minimal dependencies — designed to be easy to adopt Get started Read the Introduction for an overview and goals. Follow the Getting Started guide for installation, quick examples, and building from source. Browse the API reference (generated by DocFX) for full type and member documentation.
